doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Guitar on Tony Orlando's disco recording and Rawls film song
summary: He played fills and a solo on Orlando's disco-era version of Sweets for My Sweet, which briefly charted.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: But it’s not the right kind of vowel. It’s been a fascinating conversation. Any recording, studio recording memories you’ve had of doing things — let me rephrase. If you listen to the oldies station now these days, do you ever hear yourself with any of the Lou Rawls stuff, Tony Orlando, do you ever hear stuff you played on?

Well there was a recording that I did with Tony, which it’s a surprise because you almost never hear this thing, but Tony was trying to get into, and this was not good timing, into disco, while disco was dying. And so they made this disco recording and I had just joined the band. And for some reason they thought it was magic, he had to have me on this recording somewhere. And the road musicians don’t usually play on the recording, they have studio musicians who know how to make records rather than guys that play out. That’s just the thing in Los Angeles. But in any event so he brought me in on this arrangement to be a soloist on a song called “Sweets for my Sweet/Sugar for my Honey,” an old three chord rock song. And they wanted me to play some lead fills and a little solo in the middle of this thing and I was like “great, three chords.” And there wasn’t much for me to do to get in the way of everything. So but anyway I played this thing and they thought it was so wonderful that, you know, okay, this is going to be a hit. Well I don’t really know how the record industry works, because we were on the road and Tony comes running into the band’s dressing room and said “you’re not going to believe this, we entered the charts at number 42.” “What entered the charts?” “Sweets for my Sweet.” I said “entered the charts at 42?” Now what’s Billboard, 300 or something? It’s the top © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -20-

300? How does it enter the charts at 42? “Oh it’s very scientific. Very scientific.” Okay. Fine. So a couple of issues later it’s number thirty-something. 36 or 37. I said “you’re in the top 40.” I said great, I’m on a top 40 record. I hated it, but, I’m on a top 40 record. And then a couple of issues later he comes in and says “they pulled it.” I said “what do you mean they pulled it?” He said “it’s no longer in Billboard.” Out of 300 it was like 30 something, what happened? He said “oh it’s very scientific, very scientific.” So I don’t get it, how they got it in and when they pulled it out. So what I did here was all of a sudden was I did hear “Sweets for my Sweet” wait a minute, that’s me, and I could hear it on the radio, and I heard my little three notes, hey that was me, I did that. Another story which is backwards, when I was with Lou, he was going to do the theme soundtrack for a blacksploitation movie. There were a series of these things out in the 70’s. And this one was a series of stories based on a character who they called “Nigger Charlie.”
